questions.question: According to the context, which statement best describes the OLAP operation “slice”?

options.A: It removes one dimension by fixing a constant value, equivalent to a selection on a cuboid.
options.B: It creates a new cuboid by grouping lower‑level members into higher‑level hierarchies.
options.C: It rotates the axes of the cube so that rows become columns, similar to a pivot.
options.D: It extracts a sub‑cube by applying both selection and projection on multiple dimensions.

questions.explanation:
The text states that “slicing and dicing a data cube may correspond to selection and/or projection operations on a materialized cuboid” (Page 81). “Slice” fixes a constant on one dimension, i.e., a selection.

---

questions.question: In the same context, which description correctly captures the “dice” operation?

options.A: Selecting a single value for one dimension while keeping all other dimensions unchanged.
options.B: Applying selection on multiple dimensions simultaneously, possibly followed by projection.
options.C: Aggregating data from a lower level to a higher level in a dimension hierarchy.
options.D: Swapping the positions of two dimensions in the cube view.

questions.explanation:
The passage links “dice” with “selection and/or projection operations on a materialized cuboid” (Page 81), implying that dice involves restricting several dimensions at once.

---

questions.question: A query requests sales for the year 2010, grouped by **brand** and **province/state**. Which materialized cuboid should be used to answer the query with the least processing cost?

options.D: No existing cuboid can answer the query; a new one must be built.

questions.explanation:
The example (Page 81) lists Cuboid 3 exactly containing {year, brand, province/state}, matching the query dimensions and selection constant, making it the cheapest choice.

---

questions.question: To obtain a view that shows **sales by province/state** for a **fixed year = 2010**, starting from Cuboid 2 ({year, brand, country}), which sequence of OLAP operations is required?

options.A: Drill‑down on country → slice on year → project out brand.
options.B: Slice on year → roll‑up brand to province/state → project out country.
options.C: Slice on year → roll‑up country to province/state → project out brand.
options.D: Roll‑up brand to province/state → slice on year → project out country.

questions.explanation:
First, “slice” fixes year = 2010. Then “roll‑up” aggregates the location hierarchy from country to province/state. Finally, “project out” removes the irrelevant brand dimension, yielding the desired view. The operations follow the definitions discussed on Page 81.

---

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates a **drill‑down** operation in the dimension hierarchy described in the text?

options.A: Summarizing daily sales to obtain monthly sales.
options.C: Replacing the dimension “item name” with its higher level “brand”.
options.D: Filtering the cube to include only rows where “year = 2010”.

questions.explanation:
The hierarchy “day < month < quarter < year” (Page 81) shows that moving from a higher level (year) to a lower level (day) is a drill‑down.

---

questions.question: In the materialized‑cuboid selection process, the term “dominance” is used to prune candidates. Which statement correctly reflects this concept?

options.A: A cuboid dominates another if it contains a superset of the same dimensions, allowing it to answer any query the dominated cuboid can.
options.B: Dominance means the cuboid has the smallest storage size among all candidates.
options.C: A dominated cuboid is always selected because it requires the least computation.
options.D: Dominance refers to the number of hierarchical levels a cuboid aggregates.

questions.explanation:
The passage mentions “pruning the set using knowledge of ‘dominance’ relationships among the cuboids” (Page 81). Dominance implies one cuboid can answer all queries the other can because it holds a superset of dimensions.

---

questions.question: Suppose a query needs sales summed over **city** and **item name** for the year 2010. Which materialized cuboid should be chosen, and which OLAP operation must be applied to satisfy the selection condition?

options.B: Cuboid 2; roll‑up from country to city.
options.C: Cuboid 3; drill‑down from province/state to city.
options.D: None; the query requires building a new cuboid.

questions.explanation:
Cuboid 1 contains {year, item name, city} (Page 81), exactly the needed dimensions. Applying a “slice” fixes the year to 2010 (Page 81).

---

questions.question: Which OLAP operation would you use to transform the cube view from dimensions **{time, item, location}** to **{item, time, location}** without changing the data?
questions.explanation:
Changing the order of dimensions is called a “pivot” (listed among the operations in the required patterns). The context includes “pivot” as one of the standard OLAP operations.

---

questions.question: When materializing cuboids to speed up query processing, which of the following is a primary consideration according to the text?

options.A: The visual layout of the cube on the user interface.
options.B: The dominance relationships and estimated cost of using each cuboid.
options.C: The number of users accessing the cube simultaneously.
options.D: The alphabetical order of dimension names.

questions.explanation:
The passage outlines that after identifying potential cuboids, “pruning the set using knowledge of ‘dominance’ relationships… estimating the costs… selecting the cuboid with the least” (Page 81) guides materialization decisions.

---

questions.question: A data warehouse designer wants to update materialized cuboids efficiently during load and refresh. Which technique mentioned in the context should be explored?

options.C: Converting all cuboids to a single denormalized table.
options.D: Storing each cuboid as a separate file system object.

questions.explanation: The text explicitly notes that “during load and refresh, the materialized cuboids should be updated efficiently. Parallelism and incremental update techniques for this operation should be explored” (Page 78).
